headline: Lisbon Fights Dengue With Swarms of Sterile Mosquitoes
meta_description: Portugal releases 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes in Lisbon to control Asian tiger mosquito populations and reduce dengue transmission.
summary_short: Portugal has released 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes in Lisbon as part of a novel approach to controlling disease-carrying populations without pesticides.
body:
Portugal has released 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes in Lisbon to combat the Asian tiger mosquito, a species capable of transmitting dengue, Zika, and yellow fever. The third and final deployment of this experimental phase took place last Thursday in Alvalade, bringing the total number of sterile mosquitoes released across Portugal to 60,000. The approach relies on a straightforward biological principle: male mosquitoes don't bite—only females do—and when sterile males mate with wild females, no offspring result. Flood a population with enough sterile males, and reproduction rates collapse, all without pesticides or genetic modification.

Afonso Moreira, lead researcher and public health doctor at the Francisco George Public Health Unit, confirms the sterilization method is proven and safe, with a long history in agricultural pest control. This application to disease-carrying mosquitoes in European cities, however, remains relatively new. The current phase isn't yet focused on eliminating the population entirely. Instead, researchers are gathering fundamental data: how far do the released mosquitoes travel through urban areas, and how long do they survive? Moreira emphasizes that if dispersal and survival rates prove viable, a comparative study beginning in May will measure reproduction outcomes in treated zones against areas managed through conventional methods.

Crucially, the sterile insect technique isn't presented as a silver bullet. Moreira was explicit that habitat management—eliminating standing water and destroying breeding sites—remains the most direct control method and must continue running alongside the mosquito releases. The disease risk works through a simple chain: an infected person transmits a pathogen to a mosquito, which then passes it to the next person it bites. Fewer mosquitoes mean fewer opportunities for that chain to complete, making this dual approach a practical step forward in urban disease prevention.
quick_facts: 30,000 sterile male mosquitoes released in Lisbon's Alvalade neighborhood
60,000 total sterile mosquitoes deployed across Portugal
Asian tiger mosquito can carry dengue, Zika, and yellow fever
Method uses no pesticides or genetic modification
Next phase comparative study scheduled for May
